title: Lena and the Harbor
premise: Yara Vasquez, a lighthouse keeper's granddaughter scraping by on seasonal harbor work and a half-finished novel, agrees to pose as the partner of a stranger, Noa Reyes, at a family reunion to spare them both awkward questions. But the fake romance turns real just as Noa's family business moves to buy and demolish the harbor's aging lighthouse — the last anchor of Yara's fragile new life. Torn between loyalty to her community and a love that asks her to trust again, Yara must decide whether survival means protecting herself or risking everything. On the night of the last ferry of the season, she chooses the whole heart, and Noa chooses her over the family empire.
about_author: Kestrel Dunmore is the pen name of a former maritime archivist who spent a decade cataloguing coastal town records before turning to fiction. They write love stories set in places where the sea keeps its own ledger of what people owe.

chapters.title: The Lending Library of Small Steps
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Three years after a devastating betrayal, Yara tends the decommissioned lighthouse and writes a novel she can't finish. When her aunt demands she bring a partner to the Vasquez family reunion, panic sets in. The emotional beat is cautious loneliness — a woman measuring life in safe increments, terrified of the next unscheduled feeling.

chapters.title: A Stranger at the Fish Counter
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Noa Reyes, newly arrived to audit the harbor redevelopment, overhears Yara's frantic phone call and offers a deal: a fake date for the reunion in exchange for a local's guide to the town. The beat is wary chemistry — two people negotiating a transaction that neither fully believes is a transaction.

chapters.title: Dessert, and Other Point of No Return
chapters.summary: Dual POV. At the reunion, the fake date works too well: shared laughter, a dance, Noa's hand at Yara's back feeling like an answer to a question Yara forgot she asked. By dessert, the pretense has collapsed into something terrifyingly real. The beat is the vertigo of joy arriving ahead of permission.

chapters.title: What the Tide Brings In
chapters.summary: Noa's POV. Noa's firm unveils plans to demolish the lighthouse for a luxury marina — a project Noa is expected to champion. Hiding the assignment from Yara, Noa begins to feel the first corrosion of complicity. The beat is guilt as a slow leak, the theme of power's corruption introduced through small omissions.

chapters.title: The Harbor Remembers
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. The town organizes to save the lighthouse, and Yara, keeper's granddaughter, becomes its reluctant face. Her novel stalls; her real life has outgrown its plot. Noa helps with the campaign, and the intimacy deepens. The beat is purpose rekindled — Yara discovering that survival can mean fighting, not just enduring.

chapters.title: Pieces on Loan
chapters.summary: Dual POV. A storm strands Yara and Noa at the lighthouse overnight; confessions surface — Yara's past betrayal, Noa's fear of becoming their ruthless father. They give each other pieces of themselves, carefully rationed. The beat is tender but provisional, love as a loan neither dares to make permanent.

chapters.title: The Ledger
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Yara discovers Noa's role in the demolition project through a leaked memo. The betrayal lands with the weight of history repeating. She returns every borrowed piece of herself, shutting Noa out. The beat is heartbreak as arithmetic — the exact price of having trusted again, itemized.

chapters.title: Power's Inheritance
chapters.summary: Noa's POV. Noa confronts their father, who offers a promotion contingent on burying the harbor's objections — and a cold lesson: love is a liability the powerful learn to write off. Noa must choose between the empire they were built to inherit and the life they found by accident. The beat is the corruption of power made personal.

chapters.title: The Last Ferry of the Season
chapters.summary: Dual POV. The demolition vote coincides with the ferry's final autumn crossing. Noa testifies against the project, severing the family tie, then races to the dock where Yara is boarding to visit her sister — the safe step she promised herself. In the rain, Noa offers not an apology but a choice: stay and build something unmeasured. The beat is the climax, love against duty, everything staked.

chapters.title: Keeper of the Light
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. The lighthouse is granted heritage status; the town's ledger balances. Yara finishes her novel — its last line about a keeper who stopped counting steps — and writes a new first line with Noa beside her in the keeper's quarters. The beat is resolution as arrival: the whole heart, finally spent rather than lent, and worth every coin of survival it cost.
